viscose.types: Viscose comes as staple, cut to cotton-type or wool-type lengths for spinning alone or in blends, and as continuous filament for linings, satin and dress fabrics. Regular viscose has modest wet strength; high-wet-modulus variants made by modified viscose routes include modal and the older polynosic fibers. Specialty grades include flame-retardant viscose for protective and upholstery uses, dope-dyed viscose colored before spinning, and hollow or trilobal cross-sections for bulk or luster. Feedstock labels such as bamboo, eucalyptus or beech describe the pulp, not a different fiber. Branded fibers such as LENZING ECOVERO are regular viscose with producer claims about pulp sourcing and emissions. Cupro, often confused with viscose, is made by a different cuprammonium process.
viscose.fabrics: Viscose challis is a soft, lightweight plain weave, often printed, for dresses and blouses. Viscose crepe, twill and satin give fluid drape for skirts and shirts, and filament viscose is used for linings and ribbons. Viscose jersey, usually with a few percent elastane, is common in T-shirts and dresses. Viscose velvet has a dense, lustrous pile. Blends with polyester (often sold as TR suiting) combine drape with wrinkle resistance, and slub viscose and viscose-linen blends imitate linen. Much viscose staple also goes into nonwovens such as wipes and hygiene products, where its absorbency is valued.
viscose.quality: Regular viscose loses much of its strength wet, so the main quality risks are shrinkage and distortion after washing. Look for fabrics described as prewashed or preshrunk, and for firm, tight weaves; loosely woven challis can show seam slippage, where yarns pull apart at stressed seams. Heavier crepe and twill hold shape better than thin challis. Run fabric between your fingers: viscose should feel smooth and cool without a papery crispness from stiffening finishes that wash out. On US labels the fiber must be named rayon or viscose; 'bamboo' alone is unlawful, although 'rayon made from bamboo' is acceptable. Pulp-sourcing and lower-impact claims need brand or certification evidence.
pros: It drapes fluidly and has a soft, cool hand at modest cost.
It absorbs moisture well and takes dyes to deep, bright shades.
It is made from renewable cellulose and its fibers have biodegraded in aerobic water tests.
It blends easily with cotton, polyester, linen and elastane to add softness and drape.
cons: It is weak when wet, so garments can shrink, stretch or distort in washing.
It creases easily and can show water spots on some finishes.
The viscose process uses carbon disulfide, so environmental and worker outcomes depend on plant controls.
Pulp can come from poorly managed or endangered forests unless sourcing is documented.
viscose.impact: Two issues dominate. The first is forests: Canopy, an environmental group, has warned that a significant share of the wood pulped for fabrics comes from ancient and endangered forests. Its CanopyStyle initiative, launched in October 2013, asks brands and fiber producers to exclude such sources, and its annual Hot Button Report ranks producers on sourcing risk. The second is chemistry: carbon disulfide and sulfur emissions and zinc-bearing effluent depend on recovery at the plant. A 2010 life cycle study by Shen, Worrell and Patel found Austrian viscose among the lowest-impact fibers assessed, while viscose produced in Asia was comparable to PET, showing that plant and region matter more than the fiber name. Bamboo branding does not make viscose greener.
viscose.care: Follow the label closely, because many viscose items are marked hand wash, cold wash or dry clean. When washing is allowed, use 30 C or cooler on a delicate cycle or by hand, with a mild detergent, and support the wet fabric rather than wringing or twisting it. Roll in a towel to remove water, then dry flat or on a padded hanger; avoid hot tumble drying, a common cause of shrinkage. Iron at medium heat, about 150 C (two dots), on the reverse while slightly damp or through a pressing cloth, since viscose can scorch and develop shine. Test stain removers on a hidden seam, and store folded knits so they do not stretch on hangers.
faq: In most cases, yes. Soft bamboo apparel is usually viscose rayon made from bamboo pulp, and the chemistry is the same as wood-based viscose. The FTC requires such products to be labeled rayon or viscose, optionally 'made from bamboo', and has penalized retailers for calling them bamboo.

Regular viscose absorbs a lot of water, swells and loses much of its strength when wet, so agitation and heat can pull the fabric out of shape and shrink it. Cold, gentle washing, flat drying and avoiding the dryer prevent most problems; gentle steaming can recover some shrinkage.

Neither category fits exactly. Viscose is a manufactured fiber made from natural cellulose, usually wood pulp, which is chemically dissolved and regenerated. It is often called semi-synthetic or regenerated cellulose, and legally it is a manufactured fiber named rayon or viscose.
What is the difference between viscose and rayon?

In the United States, rayon is the generic name for regenerated cellulose fibers, and viscose is an acceptable name for fiber made by the viscose process. In the EU and much of the world, viscose is the standard label name. They usually describe the same fiber.
notable: In 2013 Amazon, Leon Max, Macy's and Sears agreed to pay a total of 1.26 million dollars in FTC civil penalties for labeling rayon textiles as bamboo.
In 2022 Kohl's and Walmart agreed to pay 2.5 million and 3 million dollars in civil penalties over bamboo claims, after FTC warning letters sent in 2010.
The FTC's 2010 warning letters on bamboo labeling went to 78 companies.
